etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English summe, from Old French summe, from Latin summa (“highest point; sum”), from summus (“highest”).

definitions.definition: A quantity obtained by addition or aggregation.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Numbers 1:2, columns 1–2:
quote.text: Take yee the ſumme of all the Congregation of the children of Iſrael, […]

quote.citation: a. 2004, Jimmy Wales, quotee, “Wikipedia:Prime objective”, in Wikipedia:
quote.text: "Imagine a world in which every single person on the planet is given free access to the sum of all human knowledge. That's what we're doing."

Synonyms: or in figurative use) sum total

definitions.definition: (often plural) An arithmetic computation, especially one posed to a student as an exercise (not necessarily limited to addition).

quote.citation: 1849 May – 1850 November, Charles Dickens, “The Emigrants”, in The Personal History of David Copperfield, London: Bradbury & Evans, […], published 1850, →OCLC, page 572:
quote.text: […]  a large sheet of paper  […]  covered with long sums  […]

quote.citation: 1981, Lisa Valentin, quoting Richie Benaud, “The day Richie Benaud stood up for principle over patriotism”, in Stuff‎[3], published 2015 April 11:
quote.text: "I think it was a disgraceful performance from a captain that got his sums wrong today, and I think it should never be permitted to happen again."

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 22:28, column 1:
quote.text: […] With a great ſumme obteined I this freedome.

quote.citation: 2008, BioWare, Mass Effect (Science Fiction), Redwood City: Electronic Arts, →ISBN, →OCLC, PC, scene: Noveria:
quote.text: Merchant Opold: This one promised compensation for services rendered. It humbly suggests that a sum of 250 credits would be most appropriate.Shepard: Would you have had any chance of getting this past customs without me? You can be a bit more generous.Merchant Opold: The other's words possess the discomforting ring of truth.Merchant Opold: This one could raise the sum to 500 credits. That is half this one's profit taken by the other. It can offer no more.

definitions.definition: A summary; the principal points or thoughts when viewed together; the substance.
A central idea or point; gist.
(rare or literary) The utmost degree; the greatest or most perfect realization (of some concept).

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, lines 1158–1159:
quote.text: Thus I have told thee all my State, and brought / My Storie to the ſum of earthly bliſs […]

quote.citation: 1877, Rev. Thomas H. Leale, chapter 2, in A Homiletic Commentary on the Book of Ecclesiastes‎[4], page 32:
quote.text: Our wisdom and skill cannot save us from accidents, pains, and from that sum of all fears and distresses—death.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An old English measure of corn equal to the quarter.

quote.citation: 1882, James Edwin Thorold Rogers, A History of Agriculture and Prices in England, volume 4, page 207:
quote.text: The sum is also used for the quarter, and the strike for the bushel.

quote.citation: 2005, Plato, translated by Lesley Brown, Sophist, page 250b:
quote.text: when you say that stability and change are, it's because you're summing them up together as embraced by it, and taking note of the communion each of them has with being.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Kazakh сом (som), Kyrgyz сом (som), Uyghur سوم (som), and Uzbek soʻm, all of which have the core signification “pure”, used in elliptical reference to historical coins of pure gold.

definitions.definition: The basic unit of money in Kyrgyzstan.
The basic unit of money in Uzbekistan.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Mongolian сум (sum), from Manchu ᠨᡳᡵᡠ (niru, “a large arrow, militia company, district”). Ultimately from Proto-Mongolic *sumun (“arrow”).

definitions.definition: A type of administrative district used in China, Mongolia, and Russia. In Mongolia, a sum is smaller than a province. In China, it is only used in Inner Mongolia, where it is equivalent to a township.
